Blow into this apana, brahmin; then you will get it. The earrings were brought here by the son of Airavata.
mahabharata:14:57.40	Do not feel disgust in this matter, my son, in any way; for you did this very thing in Gautama's hermitage then.
[Uttanka] "How should I know you, in connection with my teacher's hermitage? I wish to hear what I did before."
[The horse] "Know me as the teacher of the teacher, the blazing Fire. I was always honoured by you, child, for your teacher's sake.
Honoured always by you, brahmin, pure, joy of the Bhrigus, I shall do you good. Do so, without delay."
So addressed, Uttanka did as told; and Chitrabhanu, with ghee-flames, pleased, blazed up, wishing to burn.
Then, as he blew, O Bharata, a dense smoke came out of his pores, terrifying to the Naga world.
By that suddenly growing smoke, O Bharata, nothing could be made out in the Naga world, great king.
All the dwelling of Airavata, and of Vasuki and the other nagas, Janamejaya, resounded with cries of "Alas!"
Houses did not shine, shut in by smoke, like forests and mountains covered by mist, Bharata.
With eyes red from the smoke and scorched by the fire's heat, they came to learn the resolve of the very radiant Bhargava.
Hearing the resolve of that great sage of sharp radiance, all with troubled minds paid him honour by rule.
All the nagas, with folded hands, the aged and the children first, bowing their heads said, "Be gracious, blessed one."
Having appeased the brahmin, offering foot-water and guest-offering, the serpents gave him the two highly honoured divine earrings.
Then the mighty Uttanka, honoured by the nagas there, circled the fire to the right and went to his teacher's house.
Going quickly, king, to Gautama's house, he gave the two divine earrings to the teacher's wife, blameless one.
Thus by that great soul, Janamejaya, having gone round the three worlds, those two divine jewelled earrings were brought.
Such was the power of the sage Uttanka, bull of the Bharatas, joined with supreme austerity, which you ask me about.
[Vaishampayana] Having given a boon to Uttanka, Govinda went with Satyaki to Dvaraka, by swift, great horses.
Crossing lakes, rivers and many forests, he reached the lovely city of Dvaravati.
While the festival of Raivataka was going on, O great king, the lotus-eyed one arrived, followed by Yuyudhana.
That mountain, decked with varied forms, shone all round, bull among men, with golden kasha reeds.
The great mountain was adorned with fine golden garlands, flowers, garments and wishing-trees everywhere.
Adorned constantly with golden lamp-trees, it became like day in caves and spring-regions.
With varied banners and bells all round, resounding with men and women, it seemed as if singing; very beautiful to see, it was like Meru with hosts of sages.
The sound of the singing of drunken, delighted women and men, O Bharata, was like touching heaven from the king of mountains.
Then, bull of the Bharatas, having reached Krishna's presence, that king of mountains became like Shakra's abode.
Then, being honoured, he entered the auspicious house; Govinda and Satyaki went to their own house.
He entered glad of heart, after a long time abroad, having done a hard deed, like Vasava among the danavas.
As Vrishni arrived, the Bhojas, Vrishnis and Andhakas then went to meet the great soul, as the gods go to Shatakratu.
The wise one honoured them, asked after their welfare, and greeted his father and mother with joy.
Embraced and consoled by those two, the mighty-armed one sat down, surrounded by all the Vrishnis.
Rested, of great radiance, with his feet washed, Krishna, asked by his father, told him of the great battle.
[Vasudeva Shurasena's son] "You are an eyewitness, and know what is to be done, mighty-armed one; therefore tell me the battle truly, blameless one,
how that war of the great-souled Pandavas went, with Bhishma, Karna, Kripa, Drona, Shalya and others, unsurpassed,
and many other kshatriyas skilled in weapons, of various dress and form, dwelling in various lands."
So addressed by his father, the lotus-eyed one, in his mother's presence, told how the Kuru heroes met their end in battle.
[Vasudeva] "The marvellous deeds of those great-souled kshatriyas are so many they cannot be counted even in hundreds of years.
I shall tell you the chief deeds of the kings briefly, as they were, O you of immortal radiance.
Bhishma was the Kaurava general, eleven divisions' commander, among the Kauravas as Vasava among the gods.
Shikhandin, the wise leader of the Pandavas, commander of seven divisions, was protected by the wise Savyasachin.
Then Shikhandin, with Gandiva-bearing Arjuna, struck Ganga's son, who was not fighting, in the great battle with many arrows.
The sage lying on a bed of arrows then chose his time, leaving the southern course when the northern had come.
Then Drona became general, best of those who know weapons, hero of the Kaurava king, like Kavya of the lord of the daityas.
The best of the twice-born, surrounded by nine remaining akshauhinis, proud of battle, was guarded by Kripa, Vrisha and others.
Dhrishtadyumna became the leader of the Pandavas, knower of great weapons, guarded by Bhima, radiant, like Varuna by Mitra.
Surrounded by five divisions, desiring Drona, the great-minded one, remembering his father's humiliations, did a great deed in battle.
In that battle between Drona and Prishata's son, heroes who had come from many quarters mostly met their end.
That war was terrible for five days; then Drona, exhausted, fell under Dhrishtadyumna's control.
Then Karna became general of Duryodhana's army, surrounded in battle by five remaining akshauhinis.
Three divisions of the Pandava sons, guarded by Bibhatsu, remained standing, mostly with their heroes slain.
Then, approaching Partha like a moth a fire, Sauti's son died on the second terrible day.
When Karna was slain, the Kauravas, spiritless and their energy gone, surrounded the king of Madra with three divisions.
The Pandavas, with most of their vehicles destroyed and spiritless, surrounded Yudhishthira with the remaining one division.
King Yudhishthira of the Kurus killed the king of Madra, having done a very hard deed in half a day.
When Shalya was killed, the great-minded Sahadeva of immeasurable valour killed Shakuni, the instigator of the quarrel.
When Shakuni was slain, the king, Dhritarashtra's son, very dejected, with most of his soldiers slain, retreated, mace in hand.
The mighty Bhimasena followed him, enraged, and saw him standing in the water in the Dvaipayana lake.
Then, surrounding him on all sides with the remaining army, the five Pandavas sat down, glad, at the lake where he was.
Entering the water, struck sorely by words as arrows, he rose with mace in hand and stood ready for battle.
Then the king, Dhritarashtra's son, was slain in the great battle by Bhimasena by valour, as the kings looked on.
Then that Pandava army, asleep in the camp at night, was slain by Drona's son, unable to forgive his father's killing.
With sons, forces and friends lost, the five remaining Pandavas, with me and Yuyudhana as second.
Drona's son escaped from the battle along with Kripa and Bhoja, and the Kaurava Yuyutsu was freed by taking refuge with the Pandavas.
When the Kaurava king Suyodhana was slain with his followers, Vidura and Sanjaya attended the king of dharma.
So that war went on for eighteen days, lord, in which those kings of the earth were slain and dwelt in heaven."
[Vaishampayana] As they heard that hair-raising tale, O great king, the Vrishnis felt sorrow, joy and pain.
The hero passed over Abhimanyu's killing, O Bharata, thinking, "Let it not be displeasing to Vasudeva,"
and the greatly wise one thinking, "Hearing of his daughter's son's killing, let Vasudeva not be struck by a great calamity, burning with grief."
But Subhadra, seeing him skip the slaying of her son in battle, said, "Tell me, Krishna, of Subhadra's son's killing!" and fell to the ground.
Seeing her fallen on the ground, Vasudeva too fell on the earth, fainting with grief.
Then Vasudeva, filled with grief and sorrow at his daughter's son's killing, O great king, said to Krishna:

Are you not famed on earth, lotus-eyed one, as truthful? Why do you not tell me today of my daughter's son's death, slayer of foes?
mahabharata:14:60.8	Tell me truly, lord, the end of that nephew of yours: how was he, with eyes like yours, slain in battle by enemies?
mahabharata:14:60.9	Alas, Vrishni, death is hard when the time has not come for men, since my heart is not split a hundredfold by grief.
mahabharata:14:60.10	What did he say in the battle, lotus-eyed one, about his mother Subhadra, and about me, my dear fickle-eyed one?
mahabharata:14:60.11	Was he killed by enemies with his back turned from the fight? Was his face, Govinda, disfigured in battle?
mahabharata:14:60.12	That greatly radiant boy, Krishna, as if boasting before me, in his childish way told of his own victory, lord.
mahabharata:14:60.13	Was the child not disfigured by Drona, Karna, Kripa and others? Does he lie slain on the ground? Tell me that, Keshava.
mahabharata:14:60.14	My daughter's son always vied in battle with Drona, Bhishma and Karna, the best of charioteers.
To his father lamenting much, so grieved, Govinda, still more grieved, said:

His face was not disfigured at the head of battle, nor did he turn his back; and he fought a hard battle.
mahabharata:14:60.17	Having slain kings by hundreds of thousands in hosts, weary from Drona and Karna, he fell under Duhshasana's son's control.
mahabharata:14:60.18	Fighting alone against one, lord, he could not have been killed in battle even by the wielder of the thunderbolt.
mahabharata:14:60.19	When Partha was summoned to battle by the Samshaptakas, he was surrounded in the fight by Drona and others, enraged.
mahabharata:14:60.20	Then, after destroying a great number of enemies in battle, your daughter's son, Vrishni, fell under Duhshasana's son's control.
mahabharata:14:60.21	He has surely gone to heaven; cast off grief, greatly wise one; good men never sink on meeting calamity.
mahabharata:14:60.22	He who matched Drona, Karna and the others in battle, equal to Mahendra: how would he not gain heaven?
mahabharata:14:60.23	Cast off this hard-to-bear grief, and do not come under anger's sway; he, the conqueror of enemy cities, went to the goal made pure by weapons.
mahabharata:14:60.24	When that hero was slain, this sister of mine Subhadra, afflicted by grief, came to Pritha and cried out like an osprey.
mahabharata:14:60.25	Approaching Draupadi, the grieved one asked: 'Noble lady, where are all the children? I wish to see them.'
mahabharata:14:60.26	Hearing her words, all the Kuru women embraced her in their arms and wailed like those in great distress.
mahabharata:14:60.27	And the fair Subhadra said to Uttara, 'Fortunate one, where has your husband gone? Tell him that I wish him to come quickly.
mahabharata:14:60.28	Surely that son of Virata's daughter, hearing my voice, used to rush out of the house at once; why does your husband not come?
mahabharata:14:60.29	Abhimanyu, your great-chariot-fighting uncles are well; they all said you came here to fight, and are well.
mahabharata:14:60.30	Tell me of the battle as before, scourge of foes. Why do you not answer me today, as I lament?'
mahabharata:14:60.31	Hearing such lament of the Vrishni woman, Pritha, in great distress, said slowly:
mahabharata:14:60.32	'Subhadra, the boy, guarded in battle by Vasudeva, Satyaki and his father, was slain by the law of time.
mahabharata:14:60.33	Such is the law of mortals, do not grieve, joy of the Yadus; your son, hard to assail, has reached the highest goal.
mahabharata:14:60.34	You were born in a great family of great-souled kshatriyas; do not grieve, lotus-eyed one, for the fickle-eyed.
mahabharata:14:60.35	Look to Uttara, who is pregnant; do not grieve, fair one; she will soon bear a son of his.'
mahabharata:14:60.36	Having consoled her thus, Kunti, upholder of the Yadu line, giving up hard grief, arranged his funeral rite.
mahabharata:14:60.37	The knower of dharma, with leave of the king, Bhima and the twin pair like Yama, gave many gifts.
mahabharata:14:60.38	Having given many cows to brahmins, bull of the Yadus, she rejoiced, and the Vrishni woman said this to Virata's daughter:
mahabharata:14:60.39	'Daughter of Virata, you should not grieve for your husband, famous one; protect for me the child in your womb, fair-hipped one.'
mahabharata:14:60.40	Having said this, Kunti stopped, greatly radiant one, and having taken her leave I brought Subhadra here.
mahabharata:14:60.41	Thus your daughter's son met his end, Madhava; cast off grief, invincible one, and do not set your mind on sorrow.
So too Vasudeva performed the funeral rites of his sister's son, the great soul, always dear to his father.
The mighty-armed one duly fed six hundred thousand brahmins with food full of all good qualities.
The mighty-armed one, clothing them, removed the brahmins' craving for wealth; that was hair-raising, of Krishna.
As gold, cows, beds and clothes were given then, the brahmins said, "It is abundant."
Then Vasudeva, Dasharha, Baladeva and Satyaki performed Abhimanyu's shraddha, and Satyaka too; greatly afflicted with grief, they found no peace.
So too the Pandava heroes in the city of Nagasahvaya, deprived of Abhimanyu, found no peace.
For many days, O king, Virata's daughter, afflicted with grief for her husband, did not eat; that was greatly pitiable, and the embryo in her womb began to dissolve.
Then Vyasa came, knowing with divine sight, and the wise one of great radiance said to Pritha of large eyes and Uttara: "Give up this grief."

Therefore cast off grief, best of the Kurus, scourge of foes; it is not for you to doubt this, for this will not prove true.
mahabharata:14:61.14	What Krishna, the hero of the Vrishnis, said before, delight of the Kurus, will come about so; let there be no doubt in you.
mahabharata:14:61.15	He has gone to the imperishable worlds of the gods, won by himself; he should not be grieved for by you, dear one, nor by the other Kurus.
Thus addressed by the Grandsire, the righteous one with Dhananjaya gave up grief, great king, and became glad.
Your father too, wise knower of dharma, grew in that womb in due time, as the moon in the bright fortnight.
Then Vyasa urged the king, Dharma's son, to the horse sacrifice, and then vanished.
The wise king of dharma, hearing Vyasa's word, resolved, dear one, to go to bring the wealth.
[Janamejaya] "And how did he get the jewel that Marutta placed on the earth's surface? Tell me that, best of brahmins."
[Vaishampayana] Hearing Dvaipayana's words, King Yudhishthira, king of dharma, assembled all his brothers and at the right time said to Arjuna, Bhimasena and the twin sons of Madri:

Heroes, you have heard what was said out of friendship by Krishna, the great soul, the wise, wishing the Kurus' good,
mahabharata:14:62.5	by the great Vyasa, grown great in austerity, wishing prosperity for friends, a righteous teacher of marvellous deeds,
mahabharata:14:62.6	and by Bhishma, greatly wise, and the wise Govinda. Remembering that, Pandavas, I wish to do it rightly.
mahabharata:14:62.7	For that is good for all of us, for the future and the present, and what the knowers of Brahman say is good in its consequence.
mahabharata:14:62.8	This whole earth, upholders of the Kurus, is drained of jewels, and Vyasa told of Marutta's great wealth, kings.
mahabharata:14:62.9	If this is agreed by you, or you think it fit, let us all bring it; or what do you think, Bhima?

If we could obtain that wealth of Avikshit's son, lord, my view is that it will be as good as done, great king.
mahabharata:14:62.13	So let us, by prostrating to the great soul, the lord of the mountains, bring it; good fortune to you, having worshipped the matted-haired.
mahabharata:14:62.14	Having propitiated that lord, god of gods, and his attendants, we shall surely get the wealth by speech, mind and deed.
mahabharata:14:62.15	The servants of terrible aspect who guard that treasure will be under control when the bull-bannered one is pleased.
Hearing the words of Bhima as he spoke, the righteous king was very pleased, O Bharata; and Arjuna and the rest gladly said, "So be it."
The Pandavas, having resolved to fetch the jewels, ordered the army on a day of a steady star.
Then the sons of Pandu went, having had brahmins pronounce blessings and first worshipped the best of gods, Maheshvara.
With sweets, payasa, and meat cakes, and with blessings for the great soul, they set off, greatly delighted.
As they went, the best of brahmins and the townspeople, glad of mind, pronounced auspicious blessings.
Then, circling the brahmins with their fire and bowing their heads, the sons of Pandu set out.
Having taken leave of the king smitten by grief for his son, Dhritarashtra with his wife, and Pritha of large eyes,
leaving the Kaurava Yuyutsu, Dhritarashtra's son, at the root, honoured by townsmen and wise brahmins,
praised with hymns by bards, minstrels and panegyrists, surrounded by their own army as the sun by its rays,
with a white umbrella held over his head, Yudhishthira shone there like the moon on a full-moon night.
The Pandava, best of men, duly accepted on the road the blessings of victory from the delighted people.
So too the soldiers who followed the king: the din of their shouts stood blocking heaven.
The great king crossed lakes, rivers, forests and groves, and came to the mountain.
In that region where the excellent treasure lay, the Pandava king, with his soldiers, made his camp on a smooth, auspicious place, best of the Bharatas.
Placing in front brahmins endowed with austerity, learning and self-control, and the priest who had mastered Veda and Vedangas, Kaurava,
east of the camp the brahmins with the priest, having duly performed a pacifying rite, surrounded the king on all sides.

In this matter, best of brahmins, on an auspicious day under a good star, do as you think fit.
mahabharata:14:63.13	Let us not lose time by lingering here; having decided so, lords of brahmins, do what comes next.
Hearing the king's words, the brahmins with the priest, glad, wishing to please the king of dharma, said these words:
This very day is a holy star and day; we shall strive for the best of rites. Let us dwell here today by water, king, and fast today.
Hearing the words of those best of brahmins, the kings fasted the night, glad, lying on kusha grass beds, like blazing sacrificial fires at sacrifices.
Then that night passed for the great souls as they heard the brahmins' words; then at spotless dawn the best of brahmins spoke to the king, Dharma's son.
[Vaishampayana] Hearing the brahmins' words, Yudhishthira offered the proper offering to the lord.
The priest, having duly satisfied the fire with refined ghee, and made a mantra-perfected oblation, set off.
Taking flowers purified with mantras, O lord of the people, he offered a food-offering with sweets, payasa and meat.
With varied flowers and nets of high and low kinds, having rightly completed the whole sacrifice, the Veda-master afterward made a supreme food-offering to the servants.
To the lord of yakshas, Kubera, and Manibhadra, and to other yakshas and the lords of spirits,
with krisara, meat, and sesame oblations, the place of the god of gods shone greatly, O king.
Having worshipped Rudra and all his hosts, the king went with Vyasa before him to the treasure of jewels.
Having worshipped the lord of wealth, bowing and saluting, with varied flowers, cakes and krisara,
The Pandava's conveyances there, O lord of the people, were sixty thousand camels, twice a hundred times as many horses,
elephants by hundreds of thousands, and as many wagons, chariots and cow-elephants; the number of donkeys and men cannot be counted.
This was the wealth that Yudhishthira raised: sixteen, eight, twenty-four thousand, the mark of the loads.
Having loaded that wealth on these, the Pandava worshipped Mahadeva again and went to the city called after the elephant.
Permitted by Dvaipayana, putting the priest first, the best of men stayed a day's journey at a time.
That great army, facing the city, went on, tired with the weight of treasure, delighting the upholders of the Kurus.
Knowing the time of the horse sacrifice, the bull among men, as told by Dharma's son, was going to his own city.
With Rukmini's son and Yuyudhana, Charudeshna, Samba, Gada and Kritavarma,
the hero Sarana, Nishatha and Ulmuka, putting Baladeva before him, with Subhadra,
looking on Draupadi, Uttara and Pritha, and to console the kshatriya women whose lords were slain.
Seeing them arrived, King Dhritarashtra received them as is fit, and so did the great-minded Vidura.
Krishna stayed there, well worshipped, the bull among men, with the greatly radiant Vidura and also with Yuyutsu.
While the Vrishni heroes were staying there, Janamejaya, your father Parikshit, slayer of heroes, was born, O king.
That king, O great king, tormented by the Brahma weapon, was stillborn, motionless, increasing joy and sorrow.
Then Krishna, in great haste, entered the inner apartments with Yuyudhana as second, his senses and mind troubled.
Then he saw his father's sister coming quickly, crying "Run, Vasudeva!" again and again,
and behind her Draupadi and the renowned Subhadra, with the wailing and pity of the women of the family, O king.
Then, approaching Krishna, Kunti the king's daughter, tiger among kings, said, her voice choked with tears:

Vasudeva, mighty-armed, Devaki has a good son in you; you are our refuge and support, and this family depends on you.
mahabharata:14:65.16	Hero of the Yadus, this son of your sister's son, lord, was born killed by Ashvatthaman; revive him, Keshava.
mahabharata:14:65.17	For you promised that, delight of the Yadus, at the time of the reed: 'I shall revive the stillborn child,' lord.
mahabharata:14:65.18	He has been born dead, dear one; look at him, best of men, and at Uttara, Subhadra, Draupadi and me, Madhava.
mahabharata:14:65.19	Dharma's son, Bhima, Phalguna, Nakula and Sahadeva, invincible one: you should save us all.
mahabharata:14:65.20	In him the lives of the Pandavas and of me depend, and the funeral offering for Pandu, Dasharha, and for my father-in-law.
mahabharata:14:65.21	Good fortune to you; do what is dear today, Janardana, for Abhimanyu, who is dear and of like kind, even though he is dead.
mahabharata:14:65.22	Uttara used to tell what Abhimanyu said, Krishna, scourge of foes, from love for you, without doubt.
mahabharata:14:65.23	Arjuna's son once said to Virata's daughter, Dasharha: 'Fortunate one, your son will go to your uncle's family.
mahabharata:14:65.24	Going to the Vrishni and Andhaka family, he will learn archery and varied weapons and the whole science of policy.'
mahabharata:14:65.25	This, dear one, the invincible slayer of heroes, Subhadra's son, told out of love, and it was so, without doubt.
mahabharata:14:65.26	So we here bow to you, Madhusudana, and beg: for the good of this family, do the supreme good.
Having said this to Vrishni, Pritha of large eyes raised her arms in grief, and those others fell to the ground.
All of them, great king, their eyes full of tears, said, "Your sister's son has been born dead, lord."
When this was said, Janardana took hold of Kunti and consoled her as she lay fallen on the ground, O Bharata.
[Uttara] "Lotus-eyed one, look at the grandson of the wise Partha, born with his life ended, when the Kurus have been ended.
The reed raised by Drona's son for Bhimasena fell on Uttara and on me in victory.
That stays in my heart blazing, Keshava, that I do not see my son's son, invincible, lord.
You should always keep spies, unknown to others, to watch both your own realm and others', carefully and in many ways.
I shall not eat nor live; by good fortune you have come, Pandava. Do all that Krishna told you, Partha, entire.
Then the priests completed that rite, and Astika was pleased, having freed the serpents.
